sections.h2: Selling a house in Upper Moreland
sections.html:
Selling in Upper Moreland follows the usual Pennsylvania path, with one local advantage: the township's code enforcement department requires no use and occupancy certificate and no inspection when a residential or commercial property is resold. You sign an agreement of sale, deliver your disclosure statement first, pay transfer tax at recording and settle through a title company or attorney.

The township is in Montgomery County, about 13 to 15 miles north of Center City Philadelphia, with an estimated 25,880 residents. Most of it is Willow Grove-area housing built during the postwar growth that took the population from 5,103 in 1940 to 21,032 in 1960. Those years left a stock of mid-century houses, and showings tend to bring questions about the age of the roof and the original systems.

The township covers just under 8 square miles, so almost every house is a short drive from the turnpike, a rail station or a shopping strip.

Turnover is low: 89.0 percent of residents stayed in the same house for the past year. Fewer comparable sales exist as a result, so lean on recent sales on neighboring streets and not a township-wide average.

sections.h2: What buyers weigh about the location
sections.html:
Buyers will compare your house on a few local points:

  • A Pennsylvania Turnpike (I-276) interchange at Willow Grove lies within the township.
  • PA 611 (Easton Road), PA 263 (York Road) and PA 63 (Moreland Road) carry local traffic.
  • SEPTA's Warminster Line stops at Willow Grove station, and bus routes 22, 55, 310 and 95 serve the township.
  • The township handles trash and recycling through its public works department. PECO supplies power and gas, Aqua Pennsylvania supplies water, and the Upper Moreland-Hatboro Joint Sewer Authority handles sewage.

Gather recent utility bills for your seller packet, since buyers ask for them.

The code enforcement department requires no Use and Occupancy Certificate for the sale or resale of a residential or commercial property, and it requires no inspection on resale. Businesses moving into the township do have to file a Zoning Use Registration Permit.

Your own improvements are another story, because a buyer's inspector will look at them. Permit questions go to 117 Park Avenue, Willow Grove, or to 267-607-1032 or 267-607-1033, weekdays from 7:30 in the morning to 4:30 in the afternoon. The rules for open projects are short:

  • Residential permit plans are normally reviewed in about 15 working days, and two sets of plans are required.
  • Only a registered master plumber may submit a plumbing permit. An owner may do electrical work but still needs the permit.
  • A fence needs a permit, with a maximum height of 6 feet in a rear yard and 4 feet in a front yard.
  • Installing a pool requires a building permit.

Did you put up a fence, deck or pool without a permit? Ask the department how to close it out before the house goes on the market.

The Upper Moreland School District runs by grade band rather than by neighborhood elementary school. Upper Moreland Primary School takes kindergarten through grade 2, the Intermediate School covers grades 3 to 5, the Middle School covers grades 6 to 8, and Upper Moreland High School serves grades 9 to 12. Queen of Angels Regional Catholic School in Willow Grove is the area Catholic option. Families ask about these early, so work them into the listing.

The state takes 1 percent of the property's value in realty transfer tax and local governments add a share. Together that generally reaches 2 percent, which sellers and buyers usually divide. For the figure that applies to Upper Moreland and how it is collected, call the Montgomery County Recorder of Deeds.

A completed property disclosure statement, required by 68 Pa.C.S. Section 7303, has to reach the buyer before the agreement of sale is signed. The form asks about roofs, basements, termites, structural problems, plumbing, wiring and storm water facilities. Act 74 of 2026 changed the form's land item and added a flood-insurance notice, so get the current version from your agent or attorney.

Parcels with taxes unpaid from two years earlier go to the county Tax Claim Bureau's upset sales each September and December. To contest an assessment, go through the Board of Assessment Appeals, which posts the annual appeal deadline.

Settlement is when the title agent totals your payoff, unpaid tax and transfer tax and sends the deed to the recorder. Ask the title company or attorney what the recorder wants filed with it, transfer tax paperwork included.

Bring photo ID and your keys, and have your payoff letter confirmed a few days ahead. If a tenant or estate is involved, make sure whoever signs the deed has the authority to do so.

A short prep list saves time. Walk the house and note anything that was built or replaced during your ownership, such as a fence, a deck, a pool, a new panel or new plumbing, then check each against the permit rules above. Anything built without a permit is easiest to fix before a buyer's inspector finds it.

Next, gather the paper trail: roof and furnace receipts, recent utility bills, and your deed. Mid-century houses draw questions about original systems, and clear records let you answer them without hesitation. If the house is occupied by a tenant or sits in an estate, settle those details early so the agreement of sale can name a firm closing date.

sections.h2: Is a cash sale a good fit?
sections.html:
Cash makes the most sense if the house needs repairs you would rather not pay for, if you are settling an estate, or if speed beats squeezing out the last dollar. Mid-century houses often have tired roofs and mechanicals, and an as-is buyer ends the cycle of inspection and repair demands. Listing usually brings a higher price, along with showings and a financing window.

  • Collect two written offers or more and line up their closing dates.
  • Confirm who pays transfer tax and whether the buyer covers recording costs.
  • Ask for proof of funds before you sign anything.

faqs.q: Do I need a resale certificate in Upper Moreland?
faqs.a: No. The township's code enforcement department requires no Use and Occupancy Certificate for the sale or resale of residential or commercial property, and no resale inspection. Contractor-built work still needs the permits the township requires.

faqs.q: What is the typical home value in Upper Moreland?
faqs.a: Owners report a typical value of $391,600. That is a township-wide midpoint, so use recent sales close to your house to set a price.

faqs.q: Which county records a deed in Upper Moreland?
faqs.a: Montgomery County, through the Recorder of Deeds office. Your title company or attorney handles the filing, so ask them what the recorder needs with the deed, including transfer tax paperwork.

faqs.q: How do I find out who handles trash and sewer for my house?
faqs.a: The township's public works department handles trash and recycling, and the Upper Moreland-Hatboro Joint Sewer Authority provides sewage service. Buyers ask for the latest bills, so gather them before listing.

faqs.q: Can I sell an inherited house in Upper Moreland as-is?
faqs.a: Yes. The seller disclosure chapter does not cover transfers by a fiduciary handling a decedent's estate, but whoever signs still needs proper authority. Ask the estate's attorney who may sign the deed.
